The post Review: The Paring 2024 Pinot Noir and 2021 Red Blend appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
So The Paring is a funny name for a wine brand. Like you, probably, I assumed it was “The Pairing,” like, wine that is to be enjoyed with a meal, a succulent meal. But no, The Paring refers to, well, I’m not entirely sure, as the company behind the Santa Barbara County-based portfolio of wines never really explains it.

The company offers a range of bottlings. Today we check out its pinot noir and red blend, both quite affordable.

2024 The Paring Pinot Noir Santa Barbara County – Santa Barbara fruit aged in 65% French oak (35% new and 65% neutral) for 11 months. Designed to be a bold wine, this is initially a bit overwhelming, this pinot eventually settles into a surprisingly fruity groove, melding blackberry and raspberry into a juicy whole. A dusting of tea leaf and late-game cola evoke more traditional California pinot notes, becoming increasingly emphatic and clove-dusted as they develop in glass over time. Give it a good hour and you’ll find your toes dipping into notes of chocolate and nutmeg. A- / $25

2021 The Paring Red California – A Bordeaux style blend made from 60% Cabernet Sauvignon, 15% Cabernet Franc, 15% Merlot, and 10% Petit Verdot. Aged in French oak, 55% new and 45% neutral, for 22 months. Quite juicy with a nose of currants and some raisin, this dense wine feels more New World than Old, with overtones of milk chocolate and coffee adding even more of a dessert-like vibe, at least until the rather tannic conclusion arrives. Significant tannins perk their head up on the finish, however, wiping away much of the sweetness and leaving the palate coated in notes of black tea and dried herbs. An oddity, for sure. B / $25

title: Review: Larrikin Single Barrel Rye 9 Years Old
summary:

The post Review: Larrikin Single Barrel Rye 9 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Larrikin Bourbon Co. was founded by Greg Neeley, a former officer in both the Royal Australian Navy and the United States Navy. The name comes from an Australian term with a long history. During the 1860s and 1870s, “larrikin” referred to a young hooligan or troublemaker, often associated with working-class men, drinking, fighting, and a general disregard for authority. By the early 20th century, the word had taken on a more affectionate meaning. The archetypal larrikin became the irreverent Australian who disliked pretension, authority, and excessive formality. Mischievous and independent, the larrikin was not necessarily malicious.

During World War I, the image became closely associated with the Australian soldier, particularly members of the Australian Imperial Force (AIF). Australian troops were portrayed as rough, irreverent, resourceful, and willing to challenge authority. The larrikin became a more positive figure, representing someone willing to take an unconventional route to get the job done.

Based in Lawrenceburg, Kentucky, Larrikin Bourbon Co. has built a following through releases sourced from an assortment of distilleries. In the summer of 2026, the company released Larrikin Single Barrel Rye Whiskey 9 Years Old, distilled and aged in Bardstown, Kentucky. The whiskey was made from a mashbill of 64% rye, 30% corn, and 6% malted barley.

The origin of the rye remains officially undisclosed, but there is a connection to Nelson’s Green Brier. In 2016, Nashville’s Nelson’s Green Brier contracted Bardstown Bourbon Company to distill this exact mashbill. The resulting barrel heads were stamped “Belle Meade Rye” and “DSP KY-20037.”

The Nelson family resurrected the Belle Meade Bourbon brand in 2012 at Nelson’s Green Brier, using a mashbill of 64% corn, 30% rye, and 6% malted barley. In that recipe, the corn and rye percentages are reversed from those found in Larrikin’s rye whiskey.

Despite the “Belle Meade Rye” markings on the barrel heads, Belle Meade Rye was never released under that name. Nelson Brothers Straight Rye, however, uses the same mashbill. The house brand from Nelson’s Green Brier first appeared in 2023 and was bottled at 92.5 proof.

At 9 years old and 122.5 proof, Larrikin’s Single Barrel Rye brings additional age and considerably more proof to the same foundation represented by Nelson Brothers Straight Rye.

So, what does Larrikin’s nine-year-old rye bring to the glass?

Larrikin Single Barrel Rye 9 Years Old (2026) Review

The nose opens with a clear impression of orange Jell-O, followed by fresh sourdough bread that remains present in the glass. Given more time, fresh mint appears, followed later by under-ripe plums. It is one of the more interesting rye whiskey noses I’ve experienced in quite some time, even if its overall potency is somewhat limited.

That lack of potency on the nose is not an issue on the palate. Tangerine arrives immediately, followed by cinnamon as the citrus subsides. The mid-palate then moves toward Sour Patch Kids candy and glazed yeast donuts, with the latter tying back nicely to the sourdough note found on the nose. The palate is considerably more expressive than the nose suggests, offering far more intensity and range than the initial aroma might lead you to expect.

The finish brings ginger and an ever so slight touch of maple syrup before moving into the hot bite of sliced radish. That radish note quickly gives way to the sweet citrus profile of Sunny Delight orange drink.

For those who enjoy bright, zesty rye whiskeys, the palate and finish deliver exactly what you are looking for, all without the amount of oak influence one might expect from the age statement. In the mouth, the whiskey has medium viscosity and plenty of flavor. I simply wish the nose offered a little more expression to match what follows.

122.5 proof.

A- / $120

title: Review: NV Tabor Hill Blanc de Noir and Rosso di Lago
summary:
Few people associate Michigan with wine country, but the Tabor Hill Winery in the Lake Michigan Shore AVA has a fifty-year history of winemaking. They produce a range of offerings, including multiple varieties of reds, whites, sparkling, and fruit wines. Today we are trying two special new releases, including one white and one red, both…

The post Review: NV Tabor Hill Blanc de Noir and Rosso di Lago appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Few people associate Michigan with wine country, but the Tabor Hill Winery in the Lake Michigan Shore AVA has a fifty-year history of winemaking. They produce a range of offerings, including multiple varieties of reds, whites, sparkling, and fruit wines. Today we are trying two special new releases, including one white and one red, both made entirely with estate grown fruit. Let’s give them a try.

NV Tabor Hill Blanc de Noir – This is an uncommon style of wine made with pinot noir grapes but with minimal skin contact after pressing, which produces a white wine. The nose is reserved at first, but with time it becomes very nice, offering fleshy peach, orange peel, frothy cream, a floral note, and a bit of perfume. The palate follows suit with an Orange Julius note coming first followed by peach, lemon peel, and perfume. The wine has low to medium acidity and a fairly long finish. It will pair well with light fare including baked chicken and vegetables, but it is delightful on its own. As we’re moving into the holiday season, I think it would go perfectly with Thanksgiving turkey and stuffing. B+ / $45

NV Tabor Hill Rosso di Lago – Made in the style of an Italian Super Tuscan, this wine includes sangiovese, merlot, syrah, and cabernet sauvignon, and it is aged for a year in French and Hungarian oak. I’m surprised the wine doesn’t list the year grapes were harvested since the tannic varieties that make up the wine typically need time in the bottle to reach their peak. Poured in a glass, the wine is uninspiring, smelling like boozy grape juice with a pronounced herbal note of sage. Happily, the palate is more enjoyable with the herbal note still playing a big part, but it is balanced by blueberry, red currant, cranberry, and blackberry notes. The wine is quite dry, but fruity and tangy. Medium to high acidity and drying tannins provide a nice structure. I wasn’t optimistic when I first smelled this wine, but with a bit of time it shows nice character and complexity. I wouldn’t mistake it for a Super Tuscan, but I’d be happy to drink it alongside a steak or even a cheeseburger. B / $47

title: Review: Tax the Rich Bourbon and Felon Vodka
summary:
There is a certain expectation that whiskey should remain whiskey, that a bottle ought to concern itself with what is inside it and leave politics at the door. I understand the appeal. For many people, bourbon is an escape from the daily arguments of American life, and the idea of keeping politics out of the…

The post Review: Tax the Rich Bourbon and Felon Vodka appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
There is a certain expectation that whiskey should remain whiskey, that a bottle ought to concern itself with what is inside it and leave politics at the door. I understand the appeal. For many people, bourbon is an escape from the daily arguments of American life, and the idea of keeping politics out of the glass has an obvious draw.

There is just one problem with that idea: American beverage alcohol has never really been separate from politics.

From whiskey and bourbon to beer, wine, vodka and brandy, alcohol has repeatedly found itself caught up in the political arguments of the day. The issues have changed, but the relationship has remained. Taxes, trade, immigration, religion, race, gender, public health, consumer protection, urbanization, rural life and the role of government have all found their way into debates over what Americans drink, who may sell it, how it should be made and what should appear on the bottle.

The history of temperance alone makes that difficult to dispute. The movement that eventually helped bring about national Prohibition was not a brief campaign against drinking. It developed over roughly a century, beginning with early nineteenth-century temperance societies and gradually moving from calls for moderation toward total abstinence and, eventually, government prohibition. The American Temperance Society was founded in 1826, and by the late 1830s the movement was advocating abstinence from all alcoholic beverages. By the middle of the nineteenth century, prohibition had become a legislative issue, with at least 14 states adopting prohibition laws in some form by 1855.

Temperance was also tied to the major political and social divisions of its time. Protestant religious reform was central to much of the movement, while women became some of its most active organizers at a time when most women could not vote. Immigration and anti-Catholic sentiment became part of the debate as reformers criticized drinking customs associated with Irish, German, Italian and other immigrant communities. Industrialization and urbanization brought another set of arguments, with reformers attacking the saloon as a source of disorder, while employers sometimes supported temperance in the name of workplace productivity and safety. African American reformers and organizations also participated in temperance campaigns, although their reasons and political goals were not always the same as those of white prohibitionists.

Race was particularly ugly territory. In the post-Civil War South, anti-alcohol rhetoric was frequently intertwined with white-supremacist politics and the mythology surrounding Black men, sexual violence and white women. Temperance advocates and other political figures sometimes portrayed alcohol as a force that supposedly made Black men dangerous, while whiskey and the saloon became part of a larger argument about race, voting rights and social control. Frances Willard, one of the most prominent temperance leaders of the era, made racist claims about Black voters and drinking in an 1890 interview, linking whiskey, Black political participation and threats to white women.

The rhetoric also appeared in alcohol advertising and political imagery. The Library of Congress holds nineteenth-century whiskey advertisements and labels featuring caricatures of African Americans, among other subjects. In the South, temperance literature and liquor advertising could intersect with the poisonous racial mythology that portrayed Black men as sexually dangerous when drinking. Historical research has documented liquor advertisements that were attacked by white temperance advocates precisely because they depicted white women in ways those advocates claimed would incite Black men.

So political imagery on a whiskey bottle is hardly a new development. Neither is the use of alcohol as a vehicle for arguments about American identity.

The politics also reached the federal government and the regulation of what went into the bottle. The Bottled-in-Bond legislation of 1897 is a useful example. The law grew out of disputes involving adulteration, consumer confidence, taxation, American whiskey’s competition with imported spirits and the interests of distillers, rectifiers and wholesalers. Its passage followed extensive debate in Congress and lobbying from competing segments of the liquor trade. The resulting system placed bonded whiskey under federal supervision and provided consumers with a way to identify spirits made under prescribed conditions.

The Pure Food and Drugs Act of 1906 brought another major political fight over what Americans were entitled to know about the products they purchased. The law prohibited interstate commerce in adulterated and misbranded foods, drugs, drinks and liquors. It was the result of more than two decades of legislative attempts, public agitation, scientific investigation and political pressure. The House of Representatives passed the measure 240 to 17, and President Theodore Roosevelt signed it on June 30, 1906.

Alcohol was therefore not merely sitting on the sidelines while American consumer law developed. Whiskey producers, liquor dealers, temperance advocates, politicians, scientists and reformers were all arguing over what should be sold, how it should be labeled and how much authority the government should have over the marketplace.

And then there was Prohibition itself.

The Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act represented the culmination of decades of political organizing, religious activism, lobbying and electoral campaigning. Prohibition was not simply a referendum on whether Americans should drink. It was bound up with arguments over morality, immigration, race, gender, religion, federal power and the proper role of government. During the 1920s, the Ku Klux Klan also became an important force in Prohibition enforcement, using political pressure and, at times, vigilante methods. Historians have documented the relationship between the Klan and the broader dry movement, even as the Anti-Saloon League maintained its own political organization and denied some of the connections attributed to it.

Political cartoons, newspaper illustrations, advertisements, bottle labels and promotional material provided another outlet for those arguments. Alcohol appeared again and again in the visual record of American political life, whether the subject was temperance, immigration, race, urban vice, public morality, taxation or consumer protection. The bottle was often more than a container. It could also serve as a small billboard for a set of ideas.

That history matters when considering two contemporary bottles that make no attempt to hide their politics.

Blue State Spirits describes itself as a proudly progressive spirits company built around progress, conversation and political satire. Its stated mission centers on community, diversity, accountability and forward thinking, with the bottles intended to say something about the world around them as well as the liquid inside.

That puts Tax the Rich Bourbon and Felon Vodka squarely within a very old American tradition. Tax the Rich features the words “No Kings” alongside its political branding. Felon Vodka goes even further, placing an image of Donald Trump in an orange prison jumpsuit behind bars, a reference to his status as a convicted felon.

There is no real mystery about what either bottle is trying to say. The politics are right there on the label.

Blue State Spirits provided Drinkhacker with a bottle of Tax the Rich Bourbon and Felon Vodka for an unbiased review. Both bottles are likely to attract attention because of their political branding. The more interesting question, at least for the purposes of a spirits review, is what happens after the bottle is opened.

That is where the politics stop and the liquid gets its turn.

Tax the Rich Bourbon Review

Tax the Rich is a six-barrel blend distilled by Bardstown Bourbon Company from a mash bill of 68% corn, 20% wheat, and 12% malted barley. All six barrels come from Lot #20H11, filled on August 11, 2020, and dumped for blending on June 4, 2026, giving the bourbon a total maturation of 5 years, 9 months, and 24 days. The barrels were coopered by Independent Stave Co. with a #4 char and aged in palletized storage.

The nose opens with butterscotch hard candy discs, followed by juicy, ripe peaches with the peach fuzz intact. Waxy honeycomb and almond butter add to the sweet side of the profile. Spice is not a major factor here, with the nose favoring moderate sweetness instead. It is not an especially intricate nose, but it should appeal to a broad range of bourbon drinkers.

On the palate, vanilla pudding skin and toffee arrive first, followed by salted butter and almonds through the mid-palate. The mouthfeel falls just short of medium viscosity, with very little ethanol burn.

The finish brings a bit more going on, starting with light cinnamon before white pepper increases the heat. White pepper remains the primary note through the finish, mingling with honey graham crackers and light oak.

There is nothing off-putting about this bourbon. It is not an especially intricate pour, but it is enjoyable and serves its purpose. Those inclined to purchase Tax the Rich are probably not doing so in anticipation of a top-shelf bourbon. The appeal is largely tied to the story and the conversation that surrounds the bottle, and that comes with a bourbon that is more than capable of holding up its end of the bargain.

At $40, the price also works. Many political-theme bourbons currently on the market come with considerably higher price tags and less time in the barrel. If the goal is to spend $40 on a bottle that provides plenty to talk about while delivering a perfectly serviceable bourbon, there is little reason for regret. 92 proof. B / $40

Felon Vodka Review

Felon is distilled from a 100% corn mashbill by Golden Triangle in Craig, Missouri, with fermentation reaching 17 to 18% abv. A three-column system is used to distill the spirit, which reaches 190 proof. The vodka is Kosher certified at distillation, although Blue State Spirits did not maintain that certification through proofing and bottling.

The nose is light and clean, offering vanilla bean, toasted marshmallow, and faint grain. A slight floral note develops beneath the sweetness, accompanied by a small thread of ethanol.

The palate is soft and slightly sweet on entry, with a relatively neutral profile that gives way to faint grain and black pepper. For vodka, the mouthfeel is surprisingly full, with a slightly oily quality and medium body. A modest alcohol warmth develops through the mid-palate without becoming too hot.

The finish is short to medium in length, with mild warmth, dry grain, and a touch of sweetness reminiscent of candy corn. The alcohol gradually fades without leaving a harsh or bitter note.

Overall, Felon is a clean, approachable corn vodka that favors softness and sweetness rather than complexity. Vanilla, marshmallow, and grain give it more personality than the “neutral” designation might suggest. It is not an especially complex or memorable vodka, but its clean distillation, pleasant mouthfeel, and relatively soft finish make it considerably more enjoyable neat than its price point might suggest. 94 proof. B / $25

title: A Visit to Rosebank Distillery, “The King of the Lowlands”
summary:

The post A Visit to Rosebank Distillery, “The King of the Lowlands” appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Pass through Falkirk, Scotland, and it’s easy to think of two words that might otherwise sit in opposition: “sleepy” and “industrial.” Conveniently, those could describe the city’s Rosebank Distillery, a 186 year-old operation that’s today known for both its mothballed era — spanning nearly three decades — and its award-winning vintage casks.

Admittedly, my interest in Rosebank was piqued long before visiting. Over the past few years, its vintage single malts — specifically 30 and 31 year bottlings, casked before the distillery’s closure in 1993 — have raised eyebrows across the whisky world. My all-too-brief experiences with each left found memories. Even our own Chris Null wrote he would “travel a long way to give it another taste.”

So when the opportunity arose to tour Rosebank, it felt easy — reflexive, really — to opt in. With new owners, new stills, and new staff, how is the new-look operation working to capture that once-lost magic?

“The King of the Lowlands” — Rosebank’s History

It’s impossible to talk about Rosebank without at least a cursory recap of its history. The original distillery was founded in 1840. Wine merchant James Rankine purchased malting operations from a previous distillery (Camelon) and then established a new production site on the banks of the Forth & Clyde Canal. In its heyday, the canal was an important artery cutting across Scotland, trimming the journey between Edinburgh and Glasgow to around 9-10 hours each way. (Official boat traffic would stop in the 1960s.)

According to the distillery itself, it’s unclear exactly where the name “Rosebank” came from. But it was established by the time Rankine’s son Robert took over, going so far as to rebuild the distillery in 1868. (Rosebank also ceased its malting operations that year.) The distillery stayed family-owned until around World War 1 and was eventually acquired by Distillers Company Ltd. in the 1920s.

From then on, almost all Rosebank’s stocks went into blends. Yet the distiller’s whisky still built a reputation and gained significant respect, enough to earn the moniker “King of the Lowlands,” at least in some circles. The distillery did release an 8-year single malt starting in 1982.

But as the distillery today emphasizes, the industry’s fate lay with blends. A crowded market eventually contributed to Rosebank’s closure. The final casks of “original” Rosebank were filled on June 30, 1993; it’s from some of these late-80s and early-90s barrels that the distillery pulls its contemporary vintage releases.

To add insult to injury, the sleeping producer also lost its most iconic equipment. In 2008, thieves disguised in high-vision vests and hard hats broke into the facility and stole Rosebank’s three copper stills, piece by piece.

But in 2017, Rosebank got a lifeline. Family-owned Ian Macleod Distillers acquired the site and its remaining stocks, and Rosebank joined Glengoyne (acquired in 2003) and Tamdhu (acquired in 2012) to round out the company’s modern distillery portfolio. Rosebank’s refurbishment kicked off in 2020, with distillation beginning around three years later. Public tours started in June 2024.

Rosebank’s Modern Whisky Making

In many ways, Rosebank’s modern production is designed as a facsimile of its past. Grain is ground using a more than 100 year-old mill that was previously employed at Port Ellen. Fermentation times of between 62 and 72 hours result in an ~8.5% ABV wash, which then undergoes triple distillation. Low wines come off the first still at 21%, high wines at 41.5%, and new make at 77%.

Three new copper pot stills were built as nearly exact replicas of the old ones. The distillery also installed traditional worm tubs to collect and cool spirit right outside the building. Currently, that combination of triple distillation and worm tub condensation is unique in Scotch production.

The new make spirit is memorably fruity and complex, with bold notes of plum wine and an overall profile reminiscent of barley shochu. (It makes a great — if simple — old fashioned, which the distillery offers on certain tours.) The unaged whisky is casked at 63.5% abv, then aged primarily offsite at either Glengoyne or Tamdhu. A single, small on-site warehouse houses around 100 special casks for display.

Visiting Rosebank

Today, Rosebank employs 17 full time employees, around seven of whom conduct tours. The distillery offers a range of permanent tours:

  • Rosebank Reawakening: A basic guided tour, tasting of Glengoyne and Tamdhu whiskies, and samples of Rosebank new make. (£25 plus fees)
  • Discover the World’s Best Whisky: A more in-depth tour that also includes a dram of Rosebank 31 Year Single Malt. (£90 plus fees)
  • Rosebank Rekindled: Similar to the above, but swap the 31 year old for a 33 year single malt, then add in a chocolate pairing. (£95 plus fees)
  • Rosebank Revered: Rosebank’s most detailed tour at 3 hours. Includes a cocktail reception, full tour, a flight of three vintage Rosebank whiskies, and cask sampling from a newer cask filled in 2023. (£300, plus fees)

Admittedly, as a member of the media, I likely received a more detailed walkthrough and tasting than most. But after speaking with multiple tour guides, my impression was of folks happy to be peppered with questions ranging from the ultra-broad to mega-specific; whisky newbies and nerds alike seemed welcome.

Rosebank Distillery Immersive AV

For guests casually tagging along with a Scotch-obsessed friend or loved one, the visuals alone may be worth the price of admission, at least for a more basic tour. It’s pretty clear Ian Macleod spared no expense in reimagining the facility, which integrates an original, 33-meter chimney into a new glass-and-metal framework. Old floorboards were reclaimed into ceiling beams. And I was legitimately impressed by the warehouse’s lighting design and tour’s introductory video — the latter of which involves several projectors and impressively not-cheesy animation.

It will be years — decades, really — before we can accurately compare whiskies from the old and new Rosebank distilleries. But with Rosebank’s Legacy series of 30+ year old malts commanding prices between £1,600 and £2,100, touring is a much more accessible path to juxtaposing old versus new.

And for those whose wallets are feeling too padded, the gift shop also offers several distillery exclusive bottles — including an exceedingly rare 33 year old single malt, distilled back in 1989.

title: Review: Maker’s Mark Cellar Aged 2026
summary:
Four years into the Maker’s Mark Cellar Aged phenomenon, the limited-edition series of extra-old wheaters has settled in to a solid groove. As has always been the case with this whiskey, it’s a blend of double digit-aged offerings drawn from stock aged not in a hot rickhouse but in a cool limestone cave. Call it…

The post Review: Maker’s Mark Cellar Aged 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Four years into the Maker’s Mark Cellar Aged phenomenon, the limited-edition series of extra-old wheaters has settled in to a solid groove. As has always been the case with this whiskey, it’s a blend of double digit-aged offerings drawn from stock aged not in a hot rickhouse but in a cool limestone cave. Call it a cellar if you’d like.

This year’s whiskey is the oldest yet (or at least a tie with 2024 and 2025), comprised of 49% 11-year-old, 33% 12-year-old, and 18% 14-year-old stock.

Let’s dive in.

Maker’s Mark Cellar Aged 2026 Review

Toasty on the nose, with lots of wood, this is a denser and more tannic whiskey than Cellar Aged 2024 and 2025, and one that takes a little time in glass and on the palate to really settle into its groove. Intense note of anise, clove, and black pepper dominate the nose, barrel char taking hold on the whiskey with a vise-like grip. Fruit is fleeting, limited to dried, black fruits, dipped in dark chocolate.

The palate kicks off with a fairly hard edge, again bold with anise alongside tobacco, and more than a little lumberyard giving this whiskey a more frontier-adjacent quality than I can recall from previous expressions. Fruit starts to perk up about midway through the sip, apples in cinnamon and vanilla dominate before a touch of cherry joins the fun. The darker edges visible on the nose and the palate’s attack remain quite grippy throughout, however, with substantial clove, pepper, and crushed tobacco pushing heavy on the finish. As I mentioned last year, a note of cardamom lingers.

It’s more forceful than previous edition, but not much harder-edged than 2025, and as with all the whiskeys in this series, it’s well worth sampling.

112.1 proof.

A- / $175 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: Denizen Jamaican Rum Finished in Port Casks 8 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
“Hey, what this rum needs is something to make it even sweeter!” said, well, somebody must have said that, which is why Denizen must have decided to age an 8 year old Jamaican rum in Port casks.

We got a sample of this limited edition offering from Denizen’s Wanderer Series, which starts as a blend of four Jamaican rums — both pot and column distilled — aged eight years in bourbon barrels before spending 3 months in Port. It hits the bottle at a hefty 54% abv.

Denizen Jamaican Rum Finished in Port Casks 8 Years Old Review

Straight from the bottle and into the glass this is a truly unique experience, and not in the ways you would think. Rather than coming across as winey and dried-fruit-forward, the nose is thick with marzipan and spice, particularly ginger, which gives the rum a decidedly holiday vibe, with heavy aromas of well-browned butter. Time in glass evokes cinnamon toast, complete with some plump raisins studding the experience.

Similar tones evolve on the palate, which is also very buttery and spicy, weaving between fruitcake and butterscotch and back. Despite the oversized abv, the palate is surprisingly soft, well-tempered by lots of sugar and a bold banana note that comes across almost like pudding. While the nose eventually closes in a bit, the palate never lets up. The rum continues its tropical march and finishes with more almond and banana, layered heavily with ginger and nutmeg. Some barrel char notes are almost an afterthought as the rum fades away, adding just a hint of clove and anise to what is otherwise a monstrously sweet and candylike experience.

This needs to find a home in someone’s tiki cocktail repertoire pronto.

108 proof.

A- / $80

title: Review: Four Roses Experimental Series #1: Mizunara
summary:
Under its new ownership of E & J Gallo, Four Roses has wasted no time getting busy with new and unusual expressions to shake up its otherwise traditional reputation. After releasing its oldest whiskey ever earlier this year, Four Roses launched a new Experimental Series, starting off a collection that would explore flavor, maturation and production…

The post Review: Four Roses Experimental Series #1: Mizunara appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Under its new ownership of E & J Gallo, Four Roses has wasted no time getting busy with new and unusual expressions to shake up its otherwise traditional reputation. After releasing its oldest whiskey ever earlier this year, Four Roses launched a new Experimental Series, starting off a collection that would explore flavor, maturation and production techniques beyond the brand’s traditional 10-recipe framework.

This expression tells the story right in the name: It’s a six year old high-rye OBSK release that is finished in Japanese Mizunara oak barrels. (Finishing time is unstated.) These whiskeys will be available at the Four Roses Visitor Center in half-bottle formats.

Let’s give it a whirl.

Four Roses Experimental Series #1: Mizunara Review

Mizunara is known for its abilities to soften a whiskey and introduce an exotic edge, and this expression is no exception to that rule. The nose telegraphs it from the start: toasted coconut, cloves, and an Asian spice that approaches curry at times. The nose may be extremely atypical for bourbondom, even venturing into notes of rhubarb and dried cherry, but it’s never short of engaging.

The palate arrives with more sweetness than expected, more coconut, then butterscotch, then a soothing sandalwood quality coming up behind. Anise is distinct from there, fading into clove and cinnamon notes. I don’t think I’ve ever encountered this much overt spice in a Four Roses whiskey, so I’ll have to chalk that up to the finishing barrel. Time in glass (and ample introspection) help this whiskey showcase more earthy, almost gravelly notes, with a lingering heat and a growing, increasingly insistent florality. The finish speaks to rose petals dusted with baking spice, something I wouldn’t place in any country’s whiskey tradition, but which works amazingly well on this 100% unique experience.

104 proof.

A- / $55 (375ml)

content:
Portable coolers are not new, but the collapsible backpack variety is starting to make a more noticeable dent into this category. That’s where the Titan line of soft-sided coolers by Arctic Zone comes in. Arctic Zone was founded in 1986 and have been “driven by one mission: build insulated gear that outperforms expectations.” We road tested their 30 Can Collapsible Backpack Cooler With Ice Walls, the latest in their robust line of insulated gear made for being on the move. 

There needs a framing of the use case of the Titan around this particular small-framed 5’3″ Drinkhacker writer, which puts a higher bar on weight and shape for “portability.” I will lead my review with the double spoiler alert that the 5-pound weight at empty is a bit of a drag (literally) and is the only relevant ding to expect in my once-over. 

A cooler has literally one job — which is to keep things cold for as long as possible. That was my primary angle for my review which led me to conclude that tossing in 3 lbs of frozen ground beef that I needed defrosted eventually would be a very instructive approach (and self-serving). In went the bricks of vacuum sealed meat into the cavernous pouch, zipped up and perched on a window where it was guaranteed to be beaten down by direct sunlight for a few hours. 

The findings: After 6 hours, the ground beef was still solidly frozen to its very edges. (That pasta bolognese will need to be saved for another night). And this was without the ice packs inserted into the ice walls. After 24 hours, some of the edges softened. After 30 hours, it was pliable enough, and there was proof enough of the Titan’s chilling performance, and half-frozen was defrosted enough, to cease the experiment and start on that bolognese. 

Now that I’d had my makeshift way with putting the Titan to the test, it was time to turn to the bold claims outlined on the company’s their website: 

  • 30 Can Capacity: Large main compartment holds drinks, food, and ice for group outings or long days.
  • Deep Freeze Performance Insulation with Therma-Flect radiant barrier interior keeps ice for up to 2 days.
  • Leak proof, easy clean lining with Microban protection. Spills stay inside the cooler.
  • Smart Storage & Extras. Insulated front pocket for snacks, 2 mesh accessory pockets, plus a removable bottle opener.
  • Comfortable & Durable Design. Adjustable padded backpack straps and a water and stain repellent exterior built for everyday adventures.

The compartment is indeed large and with the material’s flexibility, it can accommodate all kinds of shapes and sizes of items, packed inside like misshapen Jenga bricks. Two full days of keeping ice might be a slight stretch but the 3 lbs of beef in my experiment took up only 20% of the available space — and cooled itself without additional frozen items. Add in the ice packs, and it’s credible to me that if the compartment was even at 80%, that contents would stay at near original temperature for 2 days. 

The backpack itself is very smartly designed and very cool in all the ways. It fits comfortably on the back and has a clasp on the straps that help steady the pack against your body. However, reverting to this particular reviewer’s idiosyncrasies, I would have preferred a strap at the base of the bag so that it secured at the hip and not across the chest. As mentioned, the bag already comes in at 5 lbs empty which means if I were to go on at least a two-day excursion where cold beverages would be the chef’s kiss at a summit, I’d make sure there was a sturdier companion to volunteer to be my sherpa. Because that sunset view over the canyon with an icy cold one with chilled charcuterie would actually be nice. 

A / $90 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

content:
Unlike a lot of recently released tequilas, this new expression from Patron doesn’t exactly reinvent the wheel. It’s a 100 proof version of its classic blanco, made using the same 100% agave, 100% tahona production techniques, and bottled in a traditional Patron decanter. No additives, just a higher abv — and, intriguingly, it is distilled to proof, with no dilution after the fact.

Patron 100 Silver Tequila Review

If you like Patron at 80 proof I expect you’ll like it just as much at 100 proof, though as with the original Patron, this remains a simple, straightforward expression. Lime leads the way on the nose, and, enhanced by the added alcohol, it’s even more prominent than in standard Patron. Peppery and quite yeasty, time in glass helps the tequila to build out a bready character, though always quite racy with a big citrus edge.

The palate fires up with some heat, with lime leaf again very prominent. This serves to temper some of the more agave-forward elements of traditional Patron, but only just so. The experience turns green and a bit vegetal after the citrus notes die down. From there, a tenacious white pepper character builds, adding spice to a thick layer of roasted agave notes, quite woody and increasingly earthy as the finish approaches.

The extra alcohol gives this blanco a dimension that 80-proof Patron seems to lack, if only slightly; the heavy lime character makes it perfect for more aggressive margaritas and Mexican martinis.

100 proof.

B+ / $50 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]
